title: The Pilate Stone: the governor's name in limestone
summary: A dedication found at Caesarea in 1961 reads '[PO]NTIUS PILATUS [PRAEF]ECTUS IUDA[EA]E' — his name and his title, prefect, where Tacitus calls him procurator.
body: Italian excavators led by Antonio Frova found the block reused as a step in the theatre at Caesarea Maritima, Pilate's seat of government. It records his dedication of a building (a 'Tiberieum') to the emperor. Three lines survive well enough to read his name and title.

Tacitus (Annals 15.44) calls Pilate a procurator; the stone gives the governor of Judea in his day the rank of praefectus. The Gospels use the general word hēgemōn, 'governor'. The original is in the Israel Museum; a replica stands at Caesarea.

title: The Caiaphas ossuary
summary: A richly carved limestone bone-box found in 1990 in Jerusalem's Peace Forest is inscribed 'Yehosef bar Qayafa' — Joseph son of Caiaphas — the high priest's full name as Josephus gives it.
body: Construction work south of the Old City broke into a family tomb with twelve ossuaries. The most ornate, decorated with rosettes, carries the name twice, once in the form 'Yehosef bar Qafa' and once 'Yehosef bar Qayafa', and contained the bones of a man of about sixty. Josephus names the high priest 'Joseph who was called Caiaphas'.

Greenhut, who published the tomb, identified the man as the high priest; William Horbury questioned it, on the spelling of the name. The ossuary is in the Israel Museum. In 2011 a second ossuary, naming 'Miriam daughter of Yeshua son of Caiaphas, priest of Maaziah from Beth Imri', surfaced on the antiquities market and was authenticated by the Israel Antiquities Authority, adding a priestly course to the family.

title: A crucified man's heel bone
summary: In 1968 an ossuary at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem yielded the right heel bone of a man named Yehohanan with an 11.5 cm iron nail still through it — the first physical remains of a crucifixion to be identified.
body: The nail had bent on a knot in the olive-wood cross and could not be withdrawn, so the heel was buried with it, along with a wooden plaque that had been used as a washer. The find shows crucifixion victims could receive Jewish burial, that the feet were nailed (here through the sides of the heels, one to each side of the upright), and that nails were used rather than only ropes. In John 20:25 Thomas speaks of 'the nail marks in His hands'.

Yehohanan was in his twenties and died in the first century AD, so his execution falls within a few decades of Jesus'. The initial report claimed both heels were pierced by one nail and the shins broken; re-examination in 1985 corrected that to one nail per heel and no certain leg fracture.

title: The Pool of Siloam, found in 2004
summary: Sewer repairs in 2004 exposed the monumental stepped pool at the southern tip of the City of David which its excavators identify as the pool where John says the blind man washed. Coins in the plaster date its construction to the reign of Alexander Jannaeus and its use through AD 70.
body: The Byzantine pool by Hezekiah's Tunnel had been taken for Siloam since the fifth century. The pool Reich and Shukron uncovered lies a little south-east: a trapezoidal pool over 70 m across with three flights of five steps, cut from the same first-century paving as the street that climbs to the Temple Mount. Coins of Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC) were found in the plaster, and coins of the First Revolt (AD 66–70) in the silt, bracketing its life.
Reich and Shukron read its size and steps as those of a mikveh, a ritual bath, used by pilgrims.

title: Bethesda's five colonnades
summary: John describes a pool 'with five covered colonnades'. Excavations near St Anne's church uncovered two adjoining pools, which Joachim Jeremias reconstructed with a colonnade on each side and a fifth across the dividing wall.
body: The twin pools north of the Temple Mount were partly exposed by Conrad Schick in 1888 and fully excavated by the White Fathers in the 1950s–60s. Two large reservoirs separated by a rock wall form a rectangle; in Jeremias's reconstruction porticoes ran around all four sides and along the central wall, five in all. A Roman shrine to Asclepius, the god of healing, was later built over the site.
The Copper Scroll from Qumran (3Q15), from before AD 70, names a 'Beth Eshdatayin', which Jeremias reads as 'house of the two pools' and takes to be Bethesda.

title: 'House of David' on a Syrian victory stone
summary: Fragments of an Aramaic stele found at Tel Dan in 1993–94 boast of killing the kings of Israel and of 'the House of David' (bytdwd) — the earliest reference to David outside the Bible, about a century and a half after his reign.
body: The inscription, which its editors Biran and Naveh attribute to Hazael of Damascus, around 840 BC, claims the deaths of '[Jeho]ram son of [Ahab] king of Israel' and '[Ahaz]iahu son of [Jehoram] king of the House of David'. 2 Kings 9 credits those deaths to Jehu.
The stele tells no story about David. Read as Biran and Naveh read bytdwd, it shows Judah's dynasty called 'the House of David' by its enemies in the mid-ninth century BC.

title: Hezekiah's tunnel and the workmen's inscription
summary: The 533 m water tunnel under the City of David, cut from both ends to meet in the middle, is still walkable. An inscription carved by the diggers describes the moment the two crews heard each other's picks through the rock.
body: 2 Kings 20:20 credits Hezekiah with 'the pool and the conduit' that brought the Gihon spring inside the walls before Sennacherib's siege (701 BC). In 1880 boys wading in the tunnel found a six-line Hebrew inscription near the outlet; its palaeography dates to about 700 BC. The stone is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum.
Radiometric dating of the tunnel's plaster and stalactites (2003) gave dates around 700 BC, which its authors set beside the Bible's dating of the tunnel to Hezekiah.

title: Sennacherib's own account of the siege of Jerusalem
summary: The Assyrian king's annals, on three clay prisms, say he shut Hezekiah up 'like a bird in a cage' in Jerusalem, and do not claim to have taken the city.
body: Sennacherib's third campaign (701 BC) is recorded on the Taylor Prism (British Museum), the Oriental Institute Prism (Chicago) and the Jerusalem Prism (Israel Museum). He lists 46 walled towns of Judah captured, tribute from Hezekiah, and the siege of Jerusalem — but the formula 'I conquered', used of the towns, is not used of the capital. 2 Kings 19:35–36 says the siege was lifted.
The reliefs from his palace at Nineveh showing the capture of Lachish (2 Kings 18:14, 17) are also in the British Museum.

title: The Cyrus Cylinder and the policy behind Ezra 1
summary: Cyrus's foundation deposit from Babylon (539 BC) announces that he returned captive peoples and their gods to their sanctuaries. Ezra 1 records a decree of Cyrus sending the exiles of Judah home to rebuild the temple.
body: The clay cylinder, found in 1879 and now in the British Museum, does not mention Jews or Jerusalem; it is written for Babylon's god Marduk. But it states the principle: 'I returned the images of the gods... to their places and let them dwell in eternal abodes. I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings.'
The Nabonidus Chronicle (also British Museum) independently dates the fall of Babylon to Cyrus in October 539 BC.

title: The oldest biblical text: a blessing on silver
summary: Two tiny rolled silver amulets from a tomb at Ketef Hinnom, Jerusalem (excavated 1979), carry the priestly blessing of Numbers 6 in Hebrew script of about 600 BC — four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls.
body: Unrolled with great difficulty, the strips read a shortened form of 'The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you...' along with a phrase close to Deuteronomy 7:9. Barkay, Vaughn, Lundberg and Zuckerman (2004) date them by their script to the late seventh or early sixth century BC, just before the Babylonian exile. They are in the Israel Museum.

title: What Josephus says of Herod's reign and death
summary: Josephus dates Herod's appointment and his capture of Jerusalem by the Roman consuls of the year, gives the reign as thirty-seven and thirty-four years, and says Herod died after an eclipse of the moon and before Passover. He names no year for the death; which year follows depends on how the figures are counted and which eclipse is meant (see the card on dating it).
body: Herod received the kingdom from the Romans 'on the hundred and eighty-fourth olympiad, when Caius Domitius Calvinus was consul the second time, and Caius Asinius Pollio', the consuls of 40 BC. He took Jerusalem 'when Marcus Agrippa and Caninius Gallus were consuls of Rome on the hundred eighty and fifth olympiad', the consuls of 37 BC. When he died he had reigned, 'since he had procured Antigonus to be slain, thirty-four years; but since he had been declared king by the Romans, thirty-seven'.

The night he burned the Matthias who had pulled down the golden eagle from the temple, 'there was an eclipse of the moon'. Herod's death, his funeral and the start of Archelaus's rule follow, and then 'the approach of that feast of unleavened bread … which feast is called the Passover'.

Finegan's table of the lunar eclipses between 7 and 1 BC, as Steinmann reproduces it, lists four, and NASA's catalogue gives the same dates and kinds: total on 23 March and 15 September 5 BC, partial on 13 March 4 BC (about a third of the moon's width in the umbra), and total on 10 January 1 BC. The dates are computed, not recorded; which of them Josephus means is the question the dating card sets out.

title: When Herod died — 4 BC or 1 BC
summary: Emil Schürer reckoned Herod's death to 4 BC, the date Andrew Steinmann calls the consensus of most scholars for a century. W. E. Filmer, Ernest Martin, Jack Finegan in his revised Handbook, and Steinmann reckon it to 1 BC. Both read the same figures in Josephus; they differ on how he counted the years and which eclipse he meant. Matthew and Luke put the birth of Jesus before the death, so the two reckonings move the latest date for the birth by three years.
body: The 4 BC reckoning, as Steinmann sets out Schürer's case: Herod was appointed in 40 BC and took Jerusalem in 37 BC, and Josephus's thirty-seven and thirty-four years count both the first and the last year (inclusive reckoning), ending in 4 BC. The eclipse is the partial one of 13 March 4 BC, twenty-nine days before Passover. The reigns of Herod's sons agree: Archelaus deposed in AD 6 after ten years, Antipas losing his tetrarchy in AD 39 after forty-three, Philip dying in AD 33/34 after thirty-seven, all counted from 4 BC. Timothy Barnes (1968) and P. M. Bernegger (1983) answered Filmer in defence of this reckoning; Barnes, as Steinmann reports him, argues that Gaius Caesar was in Rome when Archelaus came before Augustus, which he holds rules out the middle of 1 BC.

The 1 BC reckoning, as Steinmann argues it after Filmer (1966): Schürer's dates give Herod thirty-six and thirty-three years, not Josephus's thirty-seven and thirty-four, and Steinmann finds no inclusive reckoning elsewhere in Josephus. He counts Herod's first official year from Tishri 38 BC, after an appointment late in 39, and has him take Jerusalem in 36. The eclipse is the total one of 10 January 1 BC, about twelve weeks before Passover; Martin estimated that the events Josephus tells between the eclipse and Passover need at least fifty-four days, more than the twenty-nine of 4 BC. Steinmann takes the sons to have dated their reigns from when Herod named them his heirs, before his death. He adds that the early Christian writers place the birth after Passover 4 BC, most of them in late 3 or early 2 BC, and that Finegan's revised Handbook (1998) moved to the 1 BC death and a birth in 3/2 BC.

The AD count was devised by the monk Dionysius Exiguus in AD 525. On either reckoning his year 1 falls after Herod's death, so the birth falls 'BC'. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem 'two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the Magi' (Matthew 2:16); the text gives the death as the latest point for the birth, and gives no year.

title: 'The fifteenth year of Tiberius' — Luke's anchor date
summary: Luke dates John's ministry by six rulers at once. Tiberius succeeded Augustus on 19 August AD 14, so his fifteenth year, counted from then, is AD 28/29.
body: Augustus died on 19 August AD 14 (Suetonius, Augustus 100; Tacitus, Annals 1.5). Counting from then, Tiberius' fifteenth year runs from August AD 28 to August AD 29; if Luke used the Syrian calendar beginning in autumn, it is October AD 28 to September AD 29. Either way John's preaching begins about AD 28–29, and Jesus, 'about thirty' (3:23), was born around 6–2 BC (see the card on dating Herod's death).

The other five names Luke gives all check against inscriptions and Josephus: Pilate (prefect AD 26–36), Herod Antipas (tetrarch 4 BC–AD 39), Philip (4 BC–AD 34), Lysanias of Abilene (attested by an inscription from Abila under Tiberius), and the priests Annas and Caiaphas (AD 18–36).

title: The first time anyone writes 'Israel'
summary: An Egyptian victory hymn of about 1208 BC boasts 'Israel is laid waste, his seed is not' — the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible, and the Egyptian grammar treats Israel as a people rather than a place.
body: Flinders Petrie found the black granite stele in 1896 in Merneptah's mortuary temple at Thebes; it is now Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 31408. Cut in the pharaoh's fifth regnal year (≈1208 BC), it is mostly about a Libyan war, and only the last three lines turn to Canaan.

Line 27 lists the defeated: Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam — and then Israel. Egyptian writing tags every name with a silent 'determinative' sign saying what kind of thing it is. Ashkelon, Gezer and Yanoam each get the sign for a city-state. Israel gets the throw-stick (foreign) plus a seated man and woman over three strokes: the sign for a people. Frank Yurco reads this as an Israel in Canaan known to the scribe as a people, not a city or a kingdom.

The stele says nothing about Israel's origins, size, religion or relation to Egypt. It is a royal victory hymn, and its 'his seed is not' is a boast: Israel appears in later records. It dates a time by which the name existed.

title: Moab answers back: the Mesha Stele
summary: A Moabite king's own account of the same war that 2 Kings 3 describes — from the losing side's point of view. It names Omri king of Israel, the god Chemosh, and 'the vessels of YHWH': the earliest mention of Israel's God in an inscription.
body: The basalt block was found at Dhiban (biblical Dibon) in Jordan in August 1868 and stands today in the Louvre (AO 5066). Mesha king of Moab set it up about 840 BC to credit Chemosh with throwing off Israelite rule. 2 Kings 3:4-5 introduces the same king — 'Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder' — and the same revolt.

Mesha's version and the Bible's agree on the participants and disagree on the outcome: Mesha says 'Israel has perished forever', while 2 Kings 3 has the coalition withdrawing after Mesha sacrifices his son on the wall. Line 4-5 names 'Omri king of Israel' and his son, matching 1 Kings 16:23-28. Line 18 records that Mesha took 'the vessels of YHWH' from Nebo and dragged them before Chemosh — the earliest datable occurrence of the divine name outside the Bible.

One line is still argued over. Shortly after the discovery the stone was smashed by locals; about two-thirds of the fragments were recovered, and a paper squeeze taken beforehand preserves text now lost. Reading line 31 from that squeeze, André Lemaire proposed 'House of David' in 1994, which would make this a second witness alongside the Tel Dan stele; Israel Finkelstein, Nadav Na'aman and Thomas Römer argued in 2019 for the personal name 'Balak' instead. Later imaging work has been read both ways. Neither reading of line 31 is used elsewhere on this card.

title: Lachish: a siege seen from both sides
summary: Sennacherib covered a whole room of his palace with carvings of his assault on Lachish in 701 BC — and the ramp his engineers built is still there on the tell.
body: The Bible mentions Lachish almost in passing: Hezekiah sends his surrender terms to Sennacherib 'at Lachish' (2 Kings 18:14), and the Assyrian officers come up to Jerusalem from there. What the text passes over, Assyrian art dwells on. Austen Henry Layard excavated Room XXXVI of Sennacherib's South-West Palace at Nineveh in 1845-47 and found the walls lined with a continuous relief of one siege: siege engines climbing a ramp, archers, defenders throwing torches, files of deportees with their carts, and prisoners impaled outside the walls. The reliefs are now in the British Museum.
A caption over the king reads: 'Sennacherib, king of the world, king of Assyria, sat on a throne and the booty of Lachish passed before him.'

The tell itself supplies the other half. Tell ed-Duweir was dug by James Starkey in the 1930s and by David Ussishkin for Tel Aviv University from 1973. Against the south-west corner they uncovered what Ussishkin describes as the only Assyrian siege ramp yet found: a stone-and-rubble mound, roughly 50-60 m wide at the base, estimated by the excavators at ≈19,000 tons of stone. Behind the wall the defenders had thrown up a counter-ramp to keep the fighting above the attackers. The ground yielded more than 800 arrowheads, sling stones, scale armour and burnt debris, and the whole of city Level III was destroyed by fire. A nearby cave held the jumbled bones of roughly 1,500 people; whether they died in the siege is not known from the finds.
Yigael Yadin compared the walls, gate and towers drawn at Nineveh with the excavated plan and found they match; on his reading the relief pictures this hill, not a generic siege.

title: A Babylonian scribe dates the fall of Jerusalem to the day
summary: A clay tablet in the British Museum records Nebuchadnezzar taking 'the city of Judah' on the second of Adar in his seventh year — 16 March 597 BC. The date is the Babylonians' own.
body: Tablet BM 21946, one of the Babylonian Chronicles (ABC 5), is a terse year-by-year record of Nebuchadnezzar II's early reign. The seventh-year entry reads: 'In the month of Kislev the king of Akkad mustered his troops, marched to Hatti-land, and encamped against the city of Judah, and on the second day of the month of Adar he captured the city and seized the king. He appointed there a king of his own choice, received its heavy tribute and sent it to Babylon.'

2 Kings 24:10-17 tells the same events from inside the walls: Jehoiachin surrenders after a three-month reign, the treasuries are stripped, and Nebuchadnezzar installs Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah, renaming him Zedekiah: the chronicle's 'king of his own choice'.

Converting 2 Adar of Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year to the Julian calendar gives 15/16 March 597 BC. That conversion is a calculation, not something the tablet states: it rests on the Babylonian chronological tables of Parker and Dubberstein, which are built from dated astronomical texts. The event and the Babylonian date are evidence; the modern calendar date is a computed equivalent.

title: The exiled king on a Babylonian ration list
summary: Palace store records from Babylon list oil issued to 'Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu' and his five sons. A deposed king of Judah appears in the accounts of the empire that deposed him, still called king.
body: Robert Koldewey's German excavations at Babylon (1899-1917) recovered hundreds of administrative tablets from vaulted storerooms near the Ishtar Gate. Ernst Weidner published a group of them in 1939. They are ration dockets: so much oil, barley or grain to named recipients, dated between about 595 and 570 BC. Among the recipients are craftsmen from Tyre, Byblos, Egypt, Persia and Ionia — and a Judean royal household.

One text allots 10 sila of oil (about 8 litres) to 'Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu', and 2½ sila to be divided among his five sons, handed over through a Judean attendant. Ya'u-kinu is Jehoiachin; Yahudu is Judah. He is still given the royal title while Zedekiah reigned in Jerusalem. The Bible too dates by his exile: Ezekiel 1:2 by 'the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin', and 2 Kings 25:27 by its thirty-seventh year.

These tablets fall in Nebuchadnezzar's reign, so they are earlier than 2 Kings 25:27-30, where Evil-merodach releases Jehoiachin from prison in 561 BC and gives him 'a regular allowance for the rest of his life'. The tablets are in the Vorderasiatisches Museum (Pergamonmuseum), Berlin.

title: Two of Jeremiah's accusers, sealed in clay
summary: Jeremiah 38:1 names four officials who demanded the prophet's death. Excavations in the City of David turned up the personal seal impressions of two of them — Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur — a few metres apart in the same layer.
body: A bulla is a lump of clay pressed over the string of a rolled document and stamped with the sender's seal. The document rots; the clay survives, especially when the building burns. Eilat Mazar's excavation at the summit of the City of David found one in 2005 reading 'belonging to Yehukal son of Shelemyahu son of Shovi', and another in 2008, from the same late-Iron-Age stratum a few metres away, reading 'belonging to Gedalyahu son of Pashhur'.

Jeremiah 38:1 lists the officials who told Zedekiah the prophet should die: 'Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jehucal son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur son of Malchijah'. Jehucal also appears in 37:3 as one of the two men Zedekiah sends to ask Jeremiah to pray for the city. Mazar identifies the owners of the two seals with the two men of the same names in Jeremiah 38:1.

Both were excavated in place, in a dated layer. Other bullae with names from Jeremiah's circle, among them 'Berechiah son of Neriah the scribe', came from the antiquities market with no findspot. The bullae give names and fathers' names; they say nothing of the events of Jeremiah 38.

title: Belshazzar in the Babylonian records, and Daniel's 'third ruler'
summary: Outside Daniel and works drawing on it, Belshazzar was unknown until cuneiform tablets, deciphered from the 1850s on, named him as Nabonidus' eldest son, left in charge of Babylon. Daniel's offer of 'third ruler' is read by William Shea as third after the two of them, and by James Montgomery and Keil and Delitzsch as 'one of three'.
body: Berossus, Herodotus and the other classical sources give Babylon's last king as Nabonidus; none of them mentions a Belshazzar. Until the mid-nineteenth century Daniel 5 stood alone. William Shea notes that interpreters before then identified Belshazzar with one or another of the known Babylonian kings.

A clay cylinder from the temple of Sin at Ur (British Museum 91128) closes with Nabonidus praying for himself and for 'Belshazzar, my eldest son, the offspring of my heart'. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that the king spent years at the oasis of Tema in Arabia while 'the crown prince, the officers and the army were in Akkad'. The propaganda text known as the Verse Account says that Nabonidus 'entrusted the kingship' to him and went his way.

In Daniel 5 Belshazzar holds court in Babylon and offers 'third ruler in the kingdom' (5:7, 16, 29). William Shea (1982) reads this as third after Nabonidus and Belshazzar, the highest place Belshazzar could give, and a detail no Greek source preserved. James Montgomery (1927) and Keil and Delitzsch read the Aramaic as 'one of three', a member of a ruling board of three, as in Daniel 6:2. Shea argues against Montgomery's reading of the grammar.

Dated Babylonian documents never give Belshazzar the royal title; they call him mar sarri, 'son of the king'. Daniel calls him 'King Belshazzar'. The tablets bear on the chapter's setting, not on when the book was written: Porphyry, in the third century, held it written in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, as Jerome reports in answering him, and Jerome held it the prophet Daniel's own.

title: The Gallio inscription: a date for Paul in Corinth
summary: A letter of Claudius carved at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia and carries titles that date it to AD 52. Acts puts Paul before Gallio's tribunal in Corinth, and Jerome Murphy-O'Connor reckons the chronology of Paul's life from that date.
body: Nine fragments of an imperial letter were found at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi in the early twentieth century and are now in the Delphi Archaeological Museum. Claudius is writing about the depopulation of Delphi, and in passing refers to 'Lucius Junius Gallio, my friend and proconsul of Achaia'. This is the elder brother of the philosopher Seneca.

The letter dates itself the way Roman documents do, by the emperor's running titles: Claudius' twenty-sixth acclamation as imperator and his twelfth tribunician power. Both fall in AD 52, and the twenty-sixth acclamation narrows it to roughly the first half of that year.

Senatorial proconsuls served a single year beginning around 1 July, so on Murphy-O'Connor's reckoning Gallio was in office from mid-AD 51 to mid-AD 52 — and since the letter mentions him as already reporting on local conditions, his term had already begun. Acts 18:11 says Paul spent a year and six months in Corinth, and 18:12 places the hearing before Gallio inside that stay. Working backwards, Paul arrived in Corinth around the start of AD 50.

Murphy-O'Connor measures other dates in Paul's life forward or back from this one: the Jerusalem council, the Thessalonian and Corinthian letters, the later journeys. The margin is a year or so either way, and cards on this site that depend on it say so.

title: 'Whoever is caught has himself to blame for the death that follows'
summary: Herod's temple had a low stone fence carrying notices in Greek warning Gentiles not to go further, on pain of death. Two of those notices survive — and the charge that nearly killed Paul in Acts 21 is that he took a Greek past one.
body: Charles Clermont-Ganneau found a complete limestone block in 1871, reused in a school building near the Old City of Jerusalem; it is now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. A second, fragmentary copy was found in 1936 during roadworks outside the Lions' Gate and is in the Israel Museum. The Greek reads: 'No foreigner is to enter within the balustrade and enclosure around the temple area. Whoever is caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows.'

Josephus describes the fence they stood on: a stone screen three cubits high running round the inner courts, with notices at intervals 'in Greek and Latin characters' declaring the law of purity. He also reports that Rome, which otherwise reserved capital sentences to itself, allowed the temple authorities to enforce this one.

That is the background to Acts 21:28-29. The crowd seizes Paul shouting that he 'has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place' — Luke adds that they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city and assumed the rest. The notices spelled out the penalty for what the crowd charged: death.

Ellicott's commentary and the Expositor's Greek Testament (which names Bengel among others) connect Ephesians 2:14, 'He has torn down the dividing wall of hostility', with this barrier; Meyer reports the view without adopting it. The Greek word there (mesotoichon) is not the word on the stone, and Paul does not name the temple.

title: A first-century fishing boat from the Sea of Galilee
summary: A drought in 1986 exposed the hull of a working boat from the time of Jesus: 8.2 m long and patched together from at least ten kinds of wood.
body: Two brothers from Kibbutz Ginosar, Moshe and Yuval Lufan, spotted the outline of timbers in the exposed mud of the north-west shore in January 1986. The Israel Antiquities Authority excavated it in eleven days, encased it in polyurethane foam and floated it to shore. Conservation of the waterlogged wood took a further eleven years; it has been on display in the Yigal Allon Museum at Ginosar since 2000.

The hull is 8.2 m long, 2.3 m wide and 1.3 m at its highest preserved point, built shell-first with pegged mortise-and-tenon joints, the Mediterranean way of building a hull. Radiocarbon dating gave 40 BC ±80 years; the pottery and nails found with it point to roughly 50 BC to AD 50. The boat was in use somewhere in that window.
The builders used at least ten different species, much of it reused, and the hull had been repaired again and again before finally being stripped of anything worth salvaging and left to sink.

The excavators estimate from its dimensions that it could carry around fifteen people, an estimate rather than a figure anyone recorded. The Gospels put Jesus and the disciples in one boat (Mark 4:36). The boat is not connected to any Gospel event; it shows the size of a working boat on the lake in that period.

title: A pavement at Corinth signed by an Erastus
summary: A paving block by the theatre at Corinth records that 'Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid this at his own expense'. Paul greets an Erastus who is the city's treasurer. Whether they are the same man is disputed.
body: The block was uncovered in 1929 in the paved square north-east of the theatre at Corinth, with the letters cut deep and once filled with bronze. It reads ERASTVS PRO AEDILIT[AT]E S P STRAVIT: 'Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid [this pavement] at his own expense'. An aedile was an elected magistrate responsible for public works, and the customary price of election was a benefaction like this one. John Kent published it in 1966. Andrew Clarke calls it 'a mid-first century AD pavement', and the Heidelberg Epigraphic Database dates it AD 31–70; Meggitt holds the date not secure (below).
Romans 16:23, written from Corinth, sends greetings from 'Erastus, the city treasurer' — in Greek, ho oikonomos tes poleos. Acts 19:22 and 2 Timothy 4:20 mention an Erastus too.

Gerd Theissen argues for the identification: the name is not common at Corinth, the date fits, and the man Paul names holds a civic financial office. Justin Meggitt argues against: oikonomos is not the usual Greek for aedile (that would be agoranomos), an oikonomos was often a public slave or freedman rather than an elected magistrate, and the stone's own date is not secure. The question bears on a wider one the two also disagree over: whether the first urban churches included members of the governing class.
The inscription is evidence; the link to Romans 16 is an identification, and this card is filed as an interpretation for that reason.

title: 'Politarchs': Luke's title for Thessalonica's magistrates
summary: Acts 17 calls the magistrates of Thessalonica politarchs, a title found in no surviving Greek author. Around seventy inscriptions using it are now known, some twenty-eight of them from Thessalonica itself.
body: When the mob drags Jason before the city authorities, Luke calls them politarchai (Acts 17:6, 8). No classical author uses the word; the titles found elsewhere are archontes or strategoi.

Horsley catalogues roughly seventy non-literary attestations of the title; more than four-fifths come from Macedonia, and around twenty-eight from Thessalonica alone — the highest concentration anywhere. The best known was carved on the Vardar Gate of the city; the gate was demolished in 1876, but the inscribed block had already been removed and is in the British Museum.

title: Ahab at Qarqar: 2,000 chariots the Bible never mentions
summary: Shalmaneser III's stele from Kurkh lists the kings who met him at Qarqar on the Orontes, among them '2,000 chariots and 10,000 troops of Ahab the Israelite' — the largest chariot force in the alliance, and a battle Kings does not record.
body: Kings tells of Ahab's worship of Baal and his wars with Aram, and does not mention Assyria. In Shalmaneser's sixth year, ≈853 BC on the Assyrian eponym list, twelve kings of Syria and the coast stood together against Assyria at Qarqar, and Ahab brought more chariots than any of them — Hadad-ezer of Damascus brought 1,200, Irhulena of Hamath 700.

In 1 Kings, after defeating Ben-hadad, Ahab spared him and 'made a treaty with him' (20:34), and 'three years passed without war between Aram and Israel' (22:1). The Assyrian text names Damascus's king Hadad-ezer (Adda-idri) where Kings has Ben-hadad.
Shalmaneser claims a crushing victory. The figure of 2,000 chariots is the inscription's, not a count anyone can check.

This is the first time an Israelite king appears in a datable foreign record, and with the eponym list it helps anchor the chronology of the divided monarchy: Ahab was alive in 853 BC, and Jehu was on the throne by 841 BC (see the Black Obelisk).

title: The Black Obelisk: Jehu, 'son of Omri', bowing to Assyria
summary: A panel on Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk from Nimrud shows a man kneeling before the Assyrian king, captioned 'the payment of Jehu of Bīt-Ḫumrî' — literally 'son of Omri', though Jehu had wiped out Omri's family.
body: The caption reads: 'I received the payment of Jehu (Iāūa) of (Bīt)-Ḫumrî: silver, gold, a gold bowl, a gold tureen, gold vessels, gold pails, tin, the staffs of the king's hand, (and) spears.' Shalmaneser's annals put the tribute in his eighteenth year, ≈841 BC on the Assyrian eponym list, which in Thiele's chronology (the Reign tab) is the year Jehu took the throne.

To Assyria, Israel was Bīt-Ḫumrî, 'the house of Omri', after the dynasty that founded Samaria (1 Kings 16:24). So the scribe calls Jehu Omri's 'son' a few years after Jehu killed Omri's grandson Joram and all of Ahab's house (2 Kings 9–10). The phrase names his country, not his father; the Bible calls him 'son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi'.

Kings does not mention the tribute. It does say that 'in those days the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel' as Hazael of Damascus took its lands east of the Jordan (10:32-33), and Shalmaneser's annals for the same year record his war with Hazael.
The caption does not say whether the kneeling figure is Jehu himself or his envoy. It is the only known ancient picture of an Israelite king or his envoy.

title: Menahem's silver: Kings' Pul and Tiglath-pileser's annals
summary: Kings says Menahem paid 'Pul king of Assyria' a thousand talents. Tiglath-pileser III's own annals list 'Menahem of Samaria' among the kings who paid him, and Babylonian king lists give the Assyrian who ruled Babylon in his years as Pulu.
body: Tiglath-pileser III took the Assyrian throne in 745 BC (the Babylonian Chronicle's 'third year of Nabû-nasir') and in 729 BC made himself king of Babylon too. His annals and a stele from western Iran list the western kings who paid him: Rezin of Damascus, Hiram of Tyre, and 'Menahem of the city Samaria'.

2 Kings 15:19 calls the king who took Menahem's silver 'Pul'. Kings later calls the king of Assyria Tiglath-pileser (15:29). Babylonian king lists give the Assyrian who ruled Babylon in those years as Pulu. Whether Pul and Tiglath-pileser are one king or two is set out in its own card.

1 Chronicles 5:26 names both: 'the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tiglath-pilneser king of Assyria', with one verb in the singular. The BSB renders the 'and' as 'that is', reading one king under two names; the King James keeps 'and'.

Kings adds a detail no Assyrian text gives: Menahem raised the silver by taxing every wealthy man in Israel fifty shekels. A talent was 3,000 shekels (Exodus 38:25-26 counts 603,550 half-shekels as 100 talents and 1,775 shekels), so a thousand talents at fifty shekels a head is ≈60,000 men — a figure derived from the text's own numbers, if they are taken at face value.

title: The eclipse in the year of Bur-Sagale
summary: Assyria named each year after an official and kept the names in order. Under the year of Bur-Saggilê the list reads: 'the sun became eclipsed in the month of Simanu.' The dates the Reign tab pins through Assyria are counted along the list, and so rest on which eclipse that was.
body: Each Assyrian year bore the name of an official, its limmu or eponym, and scribes kept the names in order. Hermann Hunger notes that the list is 'preserved in several copies and versions'. Under one year it reads, in his translation: 'In the eponymy of Bur-Saggilê the sun became eclipsed in the month of Simanu.' Rodger Young reports a revolt in the city of Ashur recorded for the same year.

The list gives no year in our reckoning. NASA's canon of eclipses, computed by Fred Espenak, has a total eclipse of the sun on 15 June 763 BC (−762 in astronomers' numbering), with five minutes of totality at its greatest, at 39°N 54°E, east of the Caspian. Young reads NASA's map of its path as passing just north of Nineveh, so that the eclipse was total a few miles from the city and partial in it. Hunger dates the list's eclipse to this one; Rolf Furuli holds that others fit as well (see the card on which eclipse the list records).

Dated by that eclipse, Shalmaneser III's battle at Qarqar, where Ahab fought, falls in 853 BC, Jehu's payment in 841, and Menahem's in ≈740–738. The Reign tab's Assyrian pins are dated this way, and each would move with the eclipse. On it, Bur-Sagale's year falls in Jeroboam II's reign as Thiele reckons it (793–753).

Kings dates Jonah to Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). Young notes that, on the 763 dating, the list records a plague in 765, the eclipse and a revolt in 763, revolts in the years after, and 'peace in the land' in 758. He suggests the eclipse may be part of the reason Nineveh took Jonah's warning to heart, which would date his visit to 759 or 758 BC, and calls the correlation 'speculative'.

title: Which eclipse the eponym list records
summary: Hermann Hunger and Rodger Young date the eclipse in Bur-Sagale's year to 15 June 763 BC, and with it every year of the Assyrian list. Rolf Furuli holds that at least eight other eclipses fit the entry, and that Assyria's chronology rests on it alone.
body: Hunger (2008), answering a proposal that the eclipse was the partial one of 24 June 791 BC, checks the list against Babylonian astronomical texts that date three other years without it. A lunar eclipse recorded in Mukin-zeri's first year falls on 9 April 731 BC, and the Babylonian Chronicle sets that year beside Tiglath-pileser III's fourteenth; meetings of Mars and Mercury date Esarhaddon's second year to 679 BC and Ashurbanipal's eighteenth to 651. Counting back along the list from each gives 763 for Bur-Saggilê's year, in which, he writes, 'a total solar eclipse did take place in Assur'. Of 791 he writes that, at a magnitude of 0.75, it 'was hardly conspicuous and could have been noticed only if it was observed close to sunset.'

Young (2013) adds that the list's copies overlap Ptolemy's Canon, the second-century astronomer's list of the kings of Babylon and Persia, from 747 to 648 BC, and cites Thiele for their agreement there. He notes that NASA's path leaves Nineveh itself just outside totality, which 'has led some investigators to surmise' another eclipse, and writes that this 'is usually done to support alternative biblical chronologies'.

Furuli starts from the Bible's figures. In a 2009 post to the b-hebrew list he writes that the chronology of Judah 'is between 30 and 40 years longer than the chronology of Assyria, and the two chronologies cannot be conformed', and that where the sources differ the Assyrian is the one accepted. Only astronomical information tied to a particular year, he argues, can give an absolute chronology; for Assyria it comes once, in Bur-Sagale's year, and 'there are at least 8 other solar eclipses that can fit the data. So, the Neo-Assyrian chronology has a very weak foundation.' He sets the case out in Assyrian, Babylonian and Egyptian Chronology (2008).

title: Pul and Tiglath-pileser: one king or two
summary: Kings names Pul as the king Menahem paid and Tiglath-pileser as the king who took Naphtali. Rawlinson, Lepsius, A. H. Sayce, the Jewish Encyclopedia and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read the two as one king under two names; A. T. Jones held that the Bible names two kings.
body: The shared facts are in the card on Menahem's silver: Tiglath-pileser III's annals list Menahem among his tributaries, Babylonian king lists give the Assyrian who ruled Babylon in his years as Pulu, and 1 Chronicles 5:26 names 'Pul king of Assyria' and 'Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria' with one verb in the singular.

Emil Hirsch and Samuel Fuchs, in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), write that Pul 'appears in the list of kings as “Pulu,”' and that his identity with Tiglath-pileser, 'first suggested by Rawlinson' in 1863, 'was six years later independently established by Lepsius.' A. H. Sayce, as A. T. Jones quotes him, called 'the fact of their identity' 'now completely established', holding Pulu to be the king's own name and Tiglath-pileser the throne name he took. T. Nicol, in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), calls it 'now practically certain' (citing Schrader), and the BSB translates 1 Chronicles 5:26 on that reading: 'Pul king of Assyria (that is, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria)'.

A. T. Jones, in The Empires of the Bible (1897), reports that 'the most of the writers on this subject' make the two one, and disagrees. 'In the Bible,' he writes, 'Pul and Tiglath-Pileser are named in such a way as to appear clearly to be two distinct kings', and Sayce offers no evidence 'except in the name “Pulu”'. Those who identify them, he argues, have had to 'bring down the dates of the kings of Israel and Judah to a time where they cannot possibly belong'; he lets Pul reign to 764 or 763 and Tiglath-pileser come to the throne in Menahem's last years. He concedes that 'it is not here claimed that it is impossible' for the two names to be one man, only that 'there is more probability of mistake in the Assyrian records, or in deductions based upon them, than in the Scriptures.'

title: 'They killed Pekah, and I placed Hoshea over them'
summary: Kings says Hoshea killed Pekah and reigned in his place. Tiglath-pileser III's summary inscription tells the same coup from the other side: Pekah was killed and the Assyrian king installed Hoshea, and took ten talents of gold for it.
body: Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Damascus tried to force Judah into an anti-Assyrian alliance — the crisis behind Isaiah 7. Tiglath-pileser answered by taking Damascus and the north of Israel: Kings lists Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali (15:29), and Tiglath-pileser's own text names Gilead and Abel-šiṭṭi as 'the border of the land Bīt-Ḫumrî (Israel)'.

His summary inscription goes on: '(As for) the land Bīt-Ḫumrî (Israel), I brought to Assyria … all of its people. [I/they] killed Peqah, their king, and I placed Hoshea [as king o]ver them. I received from them ten talents of gold, … talents of silver.' The tablet is broken where the verb's subject stands, so whether it claims 'I killed' or 'they killed' cannot be read.

Kings says 'Hoshea son of Elah led a conspiracy against Pekah' (15:30); the inscription says Tiglath-pileser placed Hoshea over Israel. Kings later has Hoshea become Shalmaneser's vassal and pay him tribute, and imprisoned when he sent envoys to Egypt and withheld it (17:3-4).

title: Ahaz in Tiglath-pileser's tribute list: 'Jehoahaz of Judah'
summary: Ahaz sent the temple's silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser to buy help against Israel and Aram. An inscription from Nimrud lists 'Jehoahaz of the land Judah' among the kings who paid him — Ahaz under the full name the Bible shortens.
body: Isaiah told Ahaz, 'Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid' of Pekah and Rezin (Isaiah 7:4-9). Ahaz instead wrote to Tiglath-pileser, 'I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me', and sent him the silver and gold of the temple and palace (2 Kings 16:7-8).

A summary inscription from Nimrud lists the payment of the kings of the west, among them 'Sanīpu of the land Bīt-Ammon, Salāmānu of the land Moab, … Mitinti of the land Ashkelon, Jehoahaz of the land Judah, Qauš-malaka of the land Edom … gold, silver, tin, iron, lead, multi-colored garments'.

The Assyrian scribe writes Ia-ú-ḫa-zi, Yau-hazi: Jehoahaz, 'the LORD has grasped'. Kings and Isaiah call him only Ahaz, 'he has grasped', a short form without the divine name. Oracc's glossary labels Yau-hazi as Jehoahaz king of Israel, but the text says 'of the land Judah', and the only king of Judah in these years with that name is Ahaz.

Chronicles judges the purchase harshly: Tiglath-pileser 'came against him and oppressed him instead of strengthening him' (2 Chronicles 28:20). Kings adds that Ahaz went to Damascus to meet the Assyrian king there and had an altar copied from the one he saw (16:10).

title: Who took Samaria? Shalmaneser, Sargon, and 27,290 captives
summary: Kings names Shalmaneser as the king who besieged Samaria. The Babylonian Chronicle agrees he 'ravaged Samaria', but his successor Sargon II claimed the conquest, the 27,290 deportees and the resettlement for himself.
body: 2 Kings 17-18 says Shalmaneser besieged Samaria for three years and 'the king of Assyria' captured it in Hoshea's ninth year. The Babylonian Chronicle says of Shalmaneser V: 'He ravaged Samaria', and that he died in his fifth year (722/721 BC). Sargon II took the throne the same month.

Sargon's inscriptions at Khorsabad claim the city: 'I surrounded (and) conquered the city Samaria. I carried off as booty 27,290 of its inhabitants, conscripted fifty chariots from among them'. His Nimrud Prism adds that he 'restored the city Samaria and made it greater than before', brought there 'people from the lands that I had conquered' and set a eunuch over them as governor — what Kings describes in 17:24, with people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim.

The prism's number of deportees is damaged: what survives reads 27,280, and its editors restore a further 20,000 in the break, making 47,280. Hayim Tadmor reconstructed it so: Shalmaneser took the city as the siege ended, and Sargon, facing revolts at the start of his reign, came back to crush Samaria's part in a rising led by Hamath (≈720 BC) and deported its people. Kings names no king for the capture itself, only 'the king of Assyria'.
Isaiah 20:1 is the only place the Bible names Sargon. His own inscriptions came to light when Paul-Émile Botta began digging his palace at Khorsabad in 1843.

title: Sennacherib killed by his son
summary: Kings says Sennacherib was struck down by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer, who fled to Ararat, and Esarhaddon succeeded him. The Babylonian Chronicle records that he 'was killed by his son in a rebellion', and Esarhaddon's own account tells of his brothers' revolt and flight.
body: The Babylonian Chronicle: 'On the twentieth day of the month Tebêtu, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was killed by his son in a rebellion. For twenty-four years Sennacherib ruled Assyria. After the twentieth day of the month Tebêtu the rebellion continued in Assyria until the second day of the month Addaru. On the eighteenth day of the month Addaru Esarhaddon, his son, ascended the throne.' By its reckoning that is 681 BC.

Esarhaddon, the younger son, tells it as a succession fight. His brothers, jealous of his appointment as heir, 'plotted evil, girt (their) weapons, and in Nineveh … butted each other like kids for (the right to) exercise kingship'; when he marched on Nineveh, they 'deserted the army they relied on and fled to an unknown land'. Kings names the land: Ararat, that is Urartu, north of Assyria.

Neither Assyrian account names the killer, and the Chronicle has one son where Kings has two. Simo Parpola identified Kings' Adrammelech with Arda-Mulišši, a son of Sennacherib named in Assyrian letters.
Kings tells the murder straight after Sennacherib's return from Judah: 'He returned to Nineveh and stayed there' (19:36). The campaign was in 701 BC and the murder twenty years later.

title: Manasseh, a vassal on Assyria's lists
summary: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal each list 'Manasseh, king of Judah' among the western kings who served them — one sent building materials to Nineveh, the other troops for Egypt. Chronicles' story of his being taken to Babylon in chains has no Assyrian record.
body: Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, the longest of any king of Judah (2 Kings 21:1), and all of them under Assyria. Esarhaddon's Nineveh prism lists 'Ba'alu, king of Tyre, Manasseh, king of Judah, Qa'uš-gabri, king of Edom, Muṣurī, king of Moab' among twenty-two kings of the west and Cyprus whom he made carry timber and stone for his armoury at Nineveh.

Ashurbanipal's prism names him again, in almost the same list, among the kings who brought troops and gifts for his first march on Egypt (≈667 BC, a date reckoned from the Egyptian and Assyrian reign lengths).

2 Chronicles 33:11-13 tells that the commanders of the king of Assyria took Manasseh to Babylon with a hook and bronze shackles, and that he repented and was restored. Kings does not have the episode, and no Assyrian text mentions it. Ellicott's commentary notes that it has 'excited more scepticism among modern critics' than any other passage peculiar to Chronicles, without naming them; Barnes and the Cambridge Bible answer that Esarhaddon held court at Babylon at times, and that 'there is nothing improbable' in a prisoner being taken there. The prisms show Manasseh serving Assyria and say nothing of a captivity.

title: 'Are you better than Thebes?' Nahum and Assyria's own boast
summary: Nahum warns Nineveh that it is no safer than No-Amon, Thebes, which fell into captivity for all its water and allies. Ashurbanipal's annals record the conquest: he took Thebes 'in its entirety', and carried off two obelisks from a temple gate.
body: Thebes was the chief city of Upper Egypt, the seat of Amun's temples at Karnak and Luxor, defended by the Nile and allied, in Nahum's words, with Cush and Egypt, Put and Libya (3:9). Its kings in that age were the Kushite pharaohs.

Ashurbanipal's prism tells of his second Egyptian campaign: the Kushite king Tanutamon fled Memphis for Thebes, then fled Thebes as the Assyrians arrived, and 'with the support of (the god) Aššur and the goddess Ištar, I conquered that city (Thebes) in its entirety. Silver, gold, precious stones, … people — male and female — two tall obelisks … whose weight was 2,500 talents (and which) stood at a temple gate, I ripped (them) from where they were erected and took (them) to Assyria.'
The sack is dated ≈663 BC from the Egyptian and Assyrian reign lengths. Nahum tells Thebes' fall as past ('Yet she became an exile', 3:10) and Nineveh's as still to come.

title: The fall of Nineveh, 612 BC
summary: Nahum and Zephaniah foretell that Nineveh will be left a ruin. A Babylonian chronicle records how it happened: in 612 BC the Babylonians and the Medes besieged the city for three months, took it, and 'turned the city into a ruin heap'.
body: The Fall of Nineveh Chronicle, a tablet in the British Museum, covers the years of Nabopolassar of Babylon. For his fourteenth year (612/611 BC) it reads: 'The king of Akkad mustered his army and marched to Assyria. The king of the Medes marched towards the king of Akkad … In the month Simanu … they encamped against Nineveh. From the month Simanu until the month Âbu — for three months — they subjected the city to a heavy siege. … At that time Sin-šar-iškun, king of Assyria, died. They carried off the vast booty of the city and the temple and turned the city into a ruin heap.'

Zephaniah, prophesying under Josiah, says God 'will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as a desert' (2:13). Nahum describes the siege, with the river gates thrown open (2:6). The chronicle follows the last Assyrian king, Aššur-uballiṭ, west to Harran, which fell in 610 BC; Assyria as a power was gone.

Nineveh was never rebuilt as a city. Two centuries later Xenophon's army camped by its deserted walls; he was told the place was called Mespila and had once been a city of the Medes (Anabasis 3.4.10-12). Jonah son of Amittai, whose preaching Nineveh repented at, prophesied under Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), more than a century earlier.

title: The Lachish letters: 'the signals of Azekah have not been seen'
summary: Jeremiah says that when Babylon besieged Jerusalem only Lachish and Azekah still held out. A letter written on a potsherd at that time, found in Lachish's gate, reports that the officer is watching for Lachish's signals 'for the code of Azekah has not been seen'.
body: Jeremiah 34:7 is a snapshot: the Babylonian army was 'fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah — against Lachish and Azekah. For these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah.'

In 1935 J. L. Starkey's excavation at Lachish found a group of ink letters on potsherds (ostraca) in a guardroom by the city gate, written to the commander there, Yaush, in the last years of Judah. Ostracon 4 ends: 'One will (then) know that we are observing the smoke signals of Lachish according to the codes that my lord gave us, for the code of Azekah has (indeed) not been seen.' The letter does not say why Azekah's signal was not seen.

Ostracon 6 complains that letters from the officials in Jerusalem 'weaken your hands and cause the hands of the men to go slack'. That is the Hebrew idiom of Jeremiah 38:4, where the officials say Jeremiah 'is discouraging the warriors' — literally weakening the hands of the men of war. In the letters the officials are the ones accused of it.

title: Sanballat's sons and Johanan the high priest, in a letter from Egypt
summary: Nehemiah's enemy Sanballat and the high priest Johanan both appear in a papyrus written ≈407 BC by the Jews of Elephantine in Egypt, who had written to 'Johanan the high priest' in Jerusalem and to 'Delaiah and Shelemiah the sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria'.
body: A Jewish garrison at Elephantine, an island in the Nile at Egypt's southern border, kept its own temple to YHW (Ya'u). When it was destroyed in 410 BC, its leaders petitioned Bagohi (Bigvai in Cowley's edition), the Persian governor of Judah. A draft of their petition survives, dated 'the 20th of Marheshwan, the 17th year of Darius the king' — Darius II's seventeenth year, ≈407 BC by the usual reckoning of his reign (Cowley reckoned 408).

They say that they had already written 'to Johanan the high priest and his colleagues the priests who are in Jerusalem', without reply, and that they have now set out the matter 'in a letter in our name to Delaiah and Shelemiah the sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria'.

Nehemiah never gives Sanballat a title, only 'the Horonite' (2:10), and has him speak before 'the army of Samaria' (4:2). The papyrus calls him governor of Samaria and is addressed to his sons. Nehemiah 12:22-23 names a Johanan among the high priests descended from Nehemiah's contemporary Eliashib. One of Eliashib's grandsons had married Sanballat's daughter (13:28); the papyrus shows the Elephantine Jews writing to both families.

title: 'The righteous will live by faith' — read at Qumran before Paul
summary: A Dead Sea Scroll copied in the first century BC quotes Habakkuk line by line with its interpretation. It reads 2:4 as promising deliverance to those who keep the Law 'because of their suffering and their faith in the Teacher of Righteousness' — the verse Paul builds on for a different faith.
body: The Commentary on Habakkuk (1QpHab) is one of the seven scrolls found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947. It copies Habakkuk 1–2 paragraph by paragraph, each followed by pishro, 'its interpretation', applying the prophecy to the community's own day. The Chaldeans of Habakkuk 1:6 become the Kittim — the Romans.

On 2:4 it comments: 'Interpreted, this concerns all those who observe the Law in the House of Judah, whom God will deliver from the House of Judgment because of their suffering and because of their faith in the Teacher of Righteousness.'

Paul quotes the same half-verse twice: 'The righteous will live by faith' (Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11), setting faith in Christ against works of the Law. Hebrews 10:38 quotes it again, following the Greek. The scroll shows that the verse was already being read, before any of them, as a promise about whom God would save and why. The two readings differ over what faith is in and how it relates to keeping the Law.
The scroll writes God's name in the old Hebrew script within a text otherwise in the square script.

title: The Great Isaiah Scroll and the 'light' of Isaiah 53:11
summary: The BSB's 'He will see the light of life' follows a word the standard Hebrew text lacks. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied ≈125 BC, has it, and so does the Greek Septuagint: the servant 'will see light'.
body: The Masoretic text of Isaiah, the form copied in the medieval codices, reads 53:11 yirʾeh yisbaʿ — 'he shall see, he shall be satisfied' — with nothing for him to see. Translations made from it supply an object ('he shall see it', the JPS) or read 'see the fruit of'.

The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ), found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947, holds all 66 chapters of Isaiah in 54 columns on 7.34 metres of parchment. The Israel Museum dates it ≈125 BC, from its script — about a thousand years older than the oldest Hebrew Bibles known before. At 53:11 it reads yirʾeh ʾor, 'he will see light'.

The Septuagint, translated from a Hebrew text centuries before the medieval codices, has the same word: 'to shew him light' (Brenton's English). The BSB, like the NIV and NRSV, reads 'light'; others, such as the ESV, keep the Masoretic reading.
Elsewhere the scroll and the Masoretic text differ mostly in spelling.

title: 'Two years before the earthquake'
summary: Amos dates his words by an earthquake in Uzziah's reign, and Zechariah, two centuries later, still remembers people fleeing it. Excavators at Hazor and other sites found collapsed walls in layers of the mid-eighth century BC, which Steven Austin and his co-authors identify with it.
body: Zechariah 14:5 still refers to it after the exile: 'You will flee as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah.' Amos's visions include the land trembling and rising like the Nile (8:8), the temple's capitals struck so that the thresholds shake (9:1).

At Hazor, Yigal Yadin's excavations in the 1950s found in Stratum VI tilted and collapsed walls, fallen pillars and broken jars in place. Stratum V above it ended in a fire Yadin tied to Tiglath-pileser's conquest in 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29), so the collapse came earlier in the eighth century. Damage of similar date has been reported at Gezer, Lachish, Deir 'Alla and other sites.

Steven Austin and two co-authors argued in 2000 that these layers record one great earthquake of ≈750 BC, of magnitude ≈8 on the Dead Sea fault. Both figures are estimates, the date from the pottery and stratigraphy of the sites (to within some thirty years either way) and the magnitude from how widely the damage is spread.

Josephus, writing much later, connects the earthquake with Uzziah's burning incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16-21): a rent opened in the temple, sunlight struck the king's face, and he became leprous. That is a tradition, not something Chronicles says.
